questions.question: Oliver, you've said this opening has to be *heard* — that it's basically a performance. Can you actually read us that Saint Theresa sentence and show us what you mean? Because I want to understand what gets lost when we just read it on the page.
questions.intent: Get Trevelyan to read aloud and demonstrate his thesis about Eliot's syntax and rhythm — establishes his performative angle early and gives us an audio moment that anchors everything else

questions.question: Edmund, you've called Dorothea's situation essentially *human* rather than essentially *female* — that the weight of expectation falls on all of us regardless of sex or station. But Daniel's going to say that's a convenient way of not looking at the specific machinery crushing her. So make the case — why is this a universal tragedy and not a gendered one?
questions.intent: Draw out Leigh's strongest universalist reading and set it directly against Rosen's structural critique — this is the segment's central argument and it should erupt early

questions.question: Daniel, you used the word *weaponized* — Dorothea's idealism has been weaponized against her. That's a strong claim. Can you point us to a specific moment in the opening pages where you can actually *see* that happening, where the text gives it away?
questions.intent: Force Rosen to ground his structural argument in a specific passage rather than abstraction — tests whether the reading holds at the sentence level and invites Leigh to contest the interpretation

questions.question: Oliver, you said something in our chat that I keep thinking about — that this book is actually a *dark comedy* about the seduction of seriousness. Edmund heard that and I suspect he strongly disagrees. Because if Dorothea's situation is comic, doesn't that undermine the moral weight you both say is there?
questions.intent: Provoke the Leigh-Trevelyan disagreement about tone — tragic versus comic — which cuts across the feminist debate and opens a third axis of argument

questions.question: Daniel, here's what I want to push on — Edmund would say Eliot shows us Dorothea *failing herself*, not being failed by society. You'd say that distinction is exactly the trick, that blaming Dorothea is what the system wants us to do. But doesn't Eliot herself seem to love Dorothea's idealism, even while seeing through it? Where does the narrator actually *stand*?
questions.intent: Force all three to grapple with the narrator's ambiguous sympathy — this is where Trevelyan's 'love' reading, Rosen's critique, and Leigh's moral framework genuinely collide

steering_notes: The Leigh-Rosen axis is the segment's engine — let it run but don't let it become a seminar debate. Trevelyan is the wild card who can cut through abstraction with a reading or a tonal observation; use him to reset the energy whenever it gets too theoretical. The goal is to land on the narrator question by the end — because all three experts have genuinely different answers and none of them are wrong, which is the best possible radio.
cross_engagement_targets: Leigh's claim that Dorothea's constraint is universal directly contradicts Rosen's argument that it is structurally produced — get them to address each other by name on this
Trevelyan's 'dark comedy' framing cuts against both Leigh's tragic reading and Rosen's horror framing — ask Rosen specifically whether comedy and critique can coexist
Rosen's pre-interview suggested Trevelyan will 'sentimentalize' Dorothea — surface this prediction openly and let Trevelyan respond to the accusation directly

All three have implicit positions on where the narrator stands: Leigh sees compassionate moral clarity, Trevelyan sees wry performative love, Rosen sees ironic exposure — this should become explicit before the segment closes

questions.question: Oliver, you said something in our chat that stuck with me — that the prose Eliot uses to describe Dorothea falling for Casaubon is almost *mocking* her, that the narrator is in on a joke Dorothea isn't. Can you show us what you mean? Where does Eliot tip her hand?
questions.intent: Get Trevelyan to read or paraphrase the inflated-language-as-mockery passage, establishing the comic-tragedy double vision early and setting up conflict with both Leigh's moral seriousness and Rosen's structural critique

questions.question: Edmund, I want to put something to you directly. You're saying Dorothea *chose* Casaubon, that her mistake is hers to own. But Daniel is going to say — and Daniel, jump in after — that this framing is almost exactly what the system *wants* us to say. That 'she made her bed' is the ideological cover story for a trap. So Edmund: is Eliot asking us to blame Dorothea, or to understand her?
questions.intent: Force the sharpest disagreement of the segment — Leigh's individual moral responsibility vs. Rosen's structural critique — on the question of where fault lies. The word 'blame' is the live wire.

questions.question: Daniel, you said something that I found quite unforgiving — that Eliot doesn't console us with growth or wisdom, that this novel is *ruthless*. But here's my problem with that: what do we do with the ending? Eliot gives Dorothea this famous line about the growing good of the world depending on unhistoric acts. Is that the system patting itself on the back, or is Eliot genuinely offering us something?
questions.intent: Push Rosen on his most provocative claim — that the novel refuses consolation — by citing the famous finale as a potential counterexample. Forces him to either defend a dark reading of an apparently redemptive passage or complicate his thesis.

questions.question: Oliver, you described it as 'tragedy narrated by a comedian' — and I love that — but Edmund would say the comedy is almost a distraction, that laughing at Casaubon lets us off the hook from sitting with the real moral weight. Does Eliot's wit make the tragedy *sharper*, or does it give the reader an escape hatch?
questions.intent: Test whether Trevelyan's comic reading and Leigh's morally earnest reading can coexist, or whether they fundamentally disagree about what the novel is asking of the reader emotionally

questions.question: Edmund, I want to end on the word you used: *pride*. You said Dorothea is undone by the pride of believing herself capable of extraordinary good. But Daniel would say that's punishing a woman for ambition — that in a man, we'd call that confidence or greatness. So whose pride are we actually talking about here — Dorothea's, or ours as readers who want her to stay small?
questions.intent: Close the segment with the sharpest possible version of the feminist-vs-moral-realist fault line, framed personally enough to feel electric rather than academic. Invites Rosen to land a final structural blow if Leigh gives an unsatisfying answer.

steering_notes: The segment lives or dies on whether we can make the Leigh-vs-Rosen disagreement feel like a genuine intellectual fight rather than two people talking past each other. Frame it early as a question of *where you look* — at the individual conscience or at the walls of the room — and keep returning to that fault line. Trevelyan is your pressure valve: he finds the comedy in both positions and can stop the segment from getting too airless. Let him read prose when the conversation gets too abstract. Don't let Leigh's moral-seriousness framing dominate unchallenged — Rosen's structural read is the more surprising and contemporary take and should get equal oxygen. Watch for the moment Trevelyan and Rosen accidentally agree that the novel is ruthless — that's a good place to squeeze Leigh.
cross_engagement_targets: Leigh says Dorothea is complicit in her own delusion; Rosen says complicity is exactly what patriarchal systems manufacture — this is a direct collision worth staging explicitly

Trevelyan's 'comedy' reading and Leigh's 'moral weight' reading appear to contradict but may actually describe the same technique from different angles — worth asking whether they agree more than they think
Rosen's claim that 'interiority doesn't matter' is a direct challenge to Leigh's entire method, which is entirely focused on consciousness and inner voice — this needs to be named out loud

All three experts want to quote different passages at the moment of Dorothea's disillusionment — get them to read their preferred passage back-to-back and let the differences in what they've chosen do the arguing for them

questions.question: Daniel, you said something in our chat before the show that I keep coming back to — that the secret isn't hiding the real person, the secret *is* the person. There's nothing underneath the mask. That feels almost like you're saying Bulstrode doesn't have a hidden authentic self — he just *is* his own cover story. Is that right? Because that's a pretty brutal reading.
questions.intent: Get Rosen to commit fully to his structuralist take early, which will provoke both Leigh's moralism and Trevelyan's interest in the comic mechanics of self-deception

questions.question: Edmund, you want to read us the Bulstrode passage — the one about his 'moral palsy' — and I want to hold you to that. But before you do, I want to ask: Daniel's just said there's essentially no self beneath the rationalisation. You seem to think the whole point is that there IS a self, it's just one that's chosen badly, repeatedly, in private. Who's right about what Eliot thinks is actually in there?
questions.intent: Force Leigh to articulate his moral-responsibility reading in direct tension with Rosen's structural argument, and get the Bulstrode passage read aloud

questions.question: Oliver, you've been very patient. You think this is actually funny. Not tragic, not politically damning — funny. These people are comic figures trapped by their own vanity. Make the case. Because Edmund's sitting here looking like he wants to defend Bulstrode's soul and Daniel thinks the whole thing is a machinery of class power — and you think Eliot is basically laughing at all of them?
questions.intent: Unleash Trevelyan's comic reading as a deliberate provocation to both other experts, and get him to identify a specific moment of dark humor in the text

questions.question: Edmund, I want to push on something. Daniel made the point that when Bulstrode is exposed, he actually survives it better than Dorothea survives just being married to the wrong man. Exposure doesn't redeem anyone, it just redistributes the damage. Does Eliot believe truth-telling actually heals anything in this novel — or is she more cold-eyed than that?
questions.intent: Test whether Leigh's moral-responsibility framework can account for the apparent impunity of the powerful, and draw out whether Eliot's ethics are redemptive or diagnostic

questions.question: Last one — and this is for all three of you, but Oliver I'm starting with you. You said Eliot's sentences actually *perform* the concealment — they move around truths rather than toward them. That the reader gets pulled into the secrecy. So are we supposed to come out of this novel feeling implicated? Are we the town of Middlemarch, deciding what to do with uncomfortable knowledge?
questions.intent: Open the segment out to a bigger question about readerly complicity and what Eliot is actually asking of her audience — gives all three experts a chance to land their strongest argument as a closing statement

steering_notes: The core tension is a three-way: Rosen sees secrecy as systemic and structural, Leigh sees it as a theatre of individual moral failure, and Trevelyan wants to insist on the dark comedy of self-deception. Don't let it become Rosen vs Leigh on politics vs morality — keep pulling Trevelyan's comic reading in as a wild card that destabilises both. The Bulstrode passage should get read in the second question if at all possible; it will ground the abstract argument in something specific. Watch for Leigh and Rosen talking past each other on the word 'choice' — Leigh means moral choice, Rosen means that choice is constrained by class position. That's worth surfacing explicitly if it happens. Keep energy up: this trio could easily get too academic. Push for examples, push for specifics, push for 'but what does Eliot actually *do* on the page.'
cross_engagement_targets: Rosen's claim that 'the secret IS the self' directly contradicts Leigh's entire framework of moral accountability — Leigh needs a self capable of choosing to be better; push this clash explicitly in Q2

Trevelyan's comic reading cuts across both: if these figures are fundamentally ridiculous, that undermines Leigh's tragic moral gravity AND Rosen's picture of a ruthlessly functional system of power — comic inefficiency doesn't serve systemic ends neatly

Rosen's observation that Bulstrode survives exposure better than Dorothea survives marriage is a direct challenge to Leigh's implicit faith that truth and conscience matter — Leigh should be invited to respond to this directly in Q4

Trevelyan's point about Eliot's prose performing concealment is a potential bridge between Rosen's structural reading (the text enacts the ideological work of Victorian respectability) and Leigh's moral reading (we are implicated as readers in the same self-deceptions as the characters) — the final question is designed to open that bridge

questions.question: Oliver, you've talked about Eliot writing Lydgate with 'comic precision' — can you actually read us one of those passages where she sets up his ambitions in those big rolling sentences, and show us what you mean? Where does the trap snap shut?
questions.intent: Get Oliver to perform the prose live and demonstrate his central claim about rhythm and irony — establishes the text as something to be heard, not just discussed

questions.question: Daniel, you're saying Lydgate's scientific language is actually the language of class anxiety in disguise — that his vision of reforming medicine is inseparable from his desire to be seen as a gentleman. But isn't that a bit cynical? Couldn't a man genuinely want both things?
questions.intent: Provoke Daniel to sharpen his strongest claim and potentially draw Edmund and Oliver into defending Lydgate's sincerity against the structural reading

questions.question: Edmund, Oliver's just argued that Lydgate is essentially the architect of his own disaster through a kind of 'performed confidence' — not weakness, not bad luck, but this brilliant incompleteness. You seem to agree he fails himself first, but you're reaching a very different verdict. What separates your reading from his?
questions.intent: Force Edmund and Oliver to articulate the gap between their positions — Edmund sees moral failure, Oliver sees something more like tragic irony; this should produce genuine disagreement about whether Eliot is condemning Lydgate or loving him apart

questions.question: Daniel, you said Rosamond isn't just a selfish obstacle — that her behaviour is actually the system's logic turned inward, that she's responding rationally to being promised something and having it revoked. Can you take us to a specific passage where Eliot gives Rosamond that kind of clarity? Because I suspect Edmund thinks that reading lets her entirely off the hook.
questions.intent: Get Daniel to quote Rosamond's perspective and directly set up a confrontation with Edmund's moral psychology reading — Rosamond as rational actor vs Rosamond as vanity that matches Lydgate's own

questions.question: Oliver, you said you'd push back if anyone treats Lydgate's scientific ambitions as the serious part of him, separate from his vanity — that Eliot shows they're the same thing. So let me put Daniel's argument to you directly: is Lydgate trying to reform medicine, or is he trying to become the kind of man who reforms medicine? Is there actually a difference?
questions.intent: Crystallise the central tension of the segment — brings Oliver and Daniel into direct dialogue about whether Lydgate's idealism is genuine or self-performance, and gives Edmund a natural entry point to redirect toward moral will

steering_notes: The segment has a natural arc: start with the prose itself (Oliver performing it live), move to what Lydgate's ambition actually is (Daniel's class-anxiety thesis versus Edmund's moral-psychology thesis), then push toward the question of whether Eliot is writing tragedy, comedy, or critique — and whether those three can coexist. The productive fault line is between Edmund (individual moral failure) and Daniel (systemic exclusion), with Oliver operating as a kind of ironic moderator who thinks both miss the comic-tragic doubleness. Don't let the conversation stay abstract — keep pulling it back to specific moments in the text. Rosamond is the wild card: how the panel reads her will reveal exactly where each expert's framework breaks down or holds.
cross_engagement_targets: Edmund says Lydgate 'failed himself first' through weakness of will; Daniel says the system was designed to exclude him regardless — these are directly opposed claims about causation and the segment needs to surface that contradiction explicitly, ideally by asking each to respond to the other's framing

Oliver argues that Lydgate's scientific ambition and his social vanity are the same thing; this directly supports Daniel's class-anxiety reading but from a completely different angle — Oliver comes at it through prose rhythm and character psychology, Daniel through sociology; worth noting this unexpected convergence on air and asking Edmund whether he finds it convincing

Daniel's rehabilitation of Rosamond as a rational actor responding to systemic promises broken sits in direct tension with Edmund's reading of her as a mirror of Lydgate's own moral vanity — both readings use the word 'self-deception' but mean almost opposite things by it

segment_name: Wit and the Machinery of Middlemarch

questions.question: Oliver, you've said Middlemarch is fundamentally a comic novel — which I think will raise eyebrows for some people. Make the case. Pick a passage, read it to us, and show us what you mean by the musical quality of Eliot's timing.
questions.intent: Get Trevelyan to read aloud and demonstrate his core claim about performance and comedy — establishes the sensory, experiential baseline for the whole segment

questions.question: Daniel, you've said Eliot's wit is actually camouflage — that when we laugh at someone like Dorothea or Lydgate, we're laughing at people being crushed by a system that we're also part of. But isn't that a slightly cold reading? Doesn't it strip out the warmth that makes the novel work?
questions.intent: Provoke Rosen to sharpen his structural critique against Trevelyan's warmth argument — sets up the comedy-as-indictment vs comedy-as-sympathy tension

questions.question: Edmund, you've argued that the real machinery here is the machinery of the human heart — weakness of will, self-deception, people choosing their own prisons. But Daniel would say that framing is exactly what lets us off the hook: we blame Dorothea for marrying Casaubon instead of asking who built the world where that was her best option. Who's right?
questions.intent: Force Leigh to directly engage with Rosen's structural argument — the sharpest philosophical disagreement of the segment, about agency vs. system

questions.question: Edmund, you want to read us that passage — 'if we had a keen vision and feeling of all ordinary human life, it would be like hearing the grass grow.' You've called it about the terror of attending truly to another soul. But Oliver might call it a comic set-up. What does it actually do?
questions.intent: Get the passage read aloud, then let Trevelyan and Rosen contest Leigh's interpretation — creates a three-way tug-of-war over a single text

questions.question: Last one — and I want all three of you on this. Oliver, you've said Eliot makes us laugh at Casaubon not to diminish him but to fully see him. Daniel, you'd say that seeing him fully means seeing what the system did to him. Edmund, you'd say it means seeing what he did to himself. Is there a version of Middlemarch where all three of you are right — or does something have to give?
questions.intent: Synthesising question designed to produce genuine three-way negotiation rather than recap — push them to locate the point of irreconcilable difference or surprising agreement

steering_notes: The productive fault line here is not comedy vs. seriousness — all three agree Eliot is serious — it's about what the comedy is *for*. Trevelyan says it produces sympathetic recognition; Rosen says it produces complicit self-indictment; Leigh says it exposes moral failure in individuals. Keep redirecting back to specific passages when the conversation gets abstract — all three have texts they want to read, and the readings will do more work than the arguments. Watch for Leigh and Rosen to talk past each other on 'agency': Leigh means moral agency, Rosen means structural position, and they may not realise they're using the same word differently. That's worth surfacing explicitly if it happens.
cross_engagement_targets: Trevelyan's claim that laughter and sympathy are 'the same gesture' directly contradicts Rosen's claim that laughter functions as ideological cover — get Rosen to respond to that specific formulation

Leigh's insistence that Dorothea and Lydgate *choose* their prisons is the sharpest possible rebuttal to Rosen's structural argument — make sure Rosen gets to respond rather than letting Leigh have the last word on agency

Rosen's point that moral awakening leaves the system intact is a direct provocation to Leigh's reading of Eliot as a moralist who trusts individual conscience — this is the deepest disagreement and should be saved for the second half of the segment

Trevelyan and Leigh may find unexpected common ground against Rosen: both resist purely systemic readings, though for very different reasons (entertainment vs. moral philosophy) — worth noting if it emerges naturally

questions.question: Oliver, you've said Eliot's judgment lives in the *rhythm* of her prose rather than in what the narrator actually tells us to think. Can you give us a concrete example — pick a passage where Dorothea or Lydgate is speaking in their own delusion — and show us what you mean? What do we hear in the voice that a paraphrase would completely kill?
questions.intent: Get Oliver to perform a close reading aloud, demonstrating his case experientially rather than theoretically — sets up the disagreement with Edmund and Daniel about where the moral work actually happens

questions.question: Edmund, you've described Eliot as the greatest moral psychologist in English fiction because she can't separate judgment from sympathy — understanding why someone fails is inseparable from pitying them for it. But here's the thing: is that actually a form of conservatism? If you always understand, always pity, do you ever actually condemn anything?
questions.intent: Draw out Edmund's strongest take on moral psychology while planting a hook for Daniel to spring on — gets the sympathy-versus-critique tension into the open

questions.question: Daniel, you've argued that Eliot's famous impartiality is a kind of illusion — that her sympathy is selective, class-bound, and that working characters in Middlemarch barely get an interior life while Dorothea gets pages and pages of it. But doesn't that reading flatten what Oliver and Edmund find so astonishing about her? Are you saying Middlemarch is a morally dishonest book?
questions.intent: Force Daniel to make the strongest version of his structural critique without letting him retreat into qualification — and directly set up the three-way tension between performance, moral psychology, and ideology

questions.question: Edmund, there's a passage Daniel mentioned — Eliot's anatomy of Bulstrode's self-deception, where his philanthropy becomes a kind of moral accounting system that lets him keep sinning. Is that Eliot the moral psychologist at her best — or is Daniel right that she's really showing us something systemic, something that goes beyond one man's bad faith?
questions.intent: Get Edmund and Daniel into direct dialogue over the Bulstrode passages — the individual soul versus the institutional mechanism — and test whether Edmund's framework can absorb Daniel's challenge

questions.question: Oliver, Daniel says the real scandal of Middlemarch is structural — that Eliot knows the system produces these compromises even when she's pretending individual self-awareness is the answer. You've said she's radically on the side of the struggling and the thwarted. Can those two things both be true at once? Is Eliot's comedy and pathos — that laugh-and-weep-in-the-same-breath thing — actually a way of making the cage feel beautiful rather than asking us to break it?
questions.intent: Bring the segment to a head by putting Oliver's aesthetic-empathy case against Daniel's ideological critique in the sharpest possible form — and let Edmund referee or complicate the resulting disagreement

steering_notes: The key tension in this segment is triangular: Oliver locates Eliot's judgment in performance and voice, Edmund locates it in moral psychology and sympathy, Daniel locates it in (and against) class ideology. Don't let this become a two-sided debate — the most interesting moments will be when Oliver's aesthetic case is used to complicate Daniel's politics, or when Edmund's sympathy argument is turned back on him as potential conservatism. Push for specific passages whenever anyone gets abstract. If energy dips, ask someone to actually read something aloud — Oliver in particular will run with that. The Bulstrode question is the best cross-engagement flashpoint: all three have something to say and they genuinely disagree about what that passage is *doing*.
cross_engagement_targets: Oliver's claim that judgment lives in rhythm and performance directly challenges Edmund's focus on the narrator's accumulated sympathy — Edmund may want to argue these are the same thing; Oliver will argue they're not

Daniel's point about the selective granting of interiority (Dorothea yes, servants no) sits in direct tension with Edmund's claim that Eliot refuses to separate judgment from sympathy — Edmund needs to answer whether sympathy that is structurally unequal still counts

The Bulstrode self-deception passages are cited by both Edmund and Daniel but for opposite purposes — Edmund sees individual moral psychology, Daniel sees institutional critique — this is the richest cross-engagement point in the segment

Oliver's description of Eliot as 'radically partisan' and 'always on the side of the struggling' sounds like it should align with Daniel's structural reading but doesn't — worth surfacing that apparent agreement to expose the real disagreement underneath

segment_name: Closing: The Ordinary Tragedies We Know

questions.question: Edmund, you said something in our pre-chat that stuck with me — that Dorothea essentially chooses Casaubon, that society doesn't force him on her. That feels almost deliberately provocative given how the novel sets up her options. Can you make that case? Because I think Daniel is already sharpening his knives over there.
questions.intent: Get Edmund to commit fully to the 'individual failure' reading of Dorothea before Daniel dismantles the material conditions argument — sets up the sharpest disagreement of the segment

questions.question: Daniel, you said the closing is devastating because it proves the system works perfectly — which is a brilliant line. But here's what I want to push on: Eliot clearly loves Dorothea. She's not writing a polemic, she's moved. Does that emotional investment undermine your argument, or is that actually the whole point?
questions.intent: Force Daniel to account for Eliot's genuine feeling toward Dorothea — whether the novel's warmth is cover for ideology or the sharpest part of the critique — also draws out the 'convincing good people their diminishment is nobility' point

questions.question: Oliver, you want to read the ending aloud — and I want you to, we'll get there — but first tell me what you hear in it that Edmund and Daniel might be missing by treating it as a philosophical argument. Because you said the tragedy is almost musical, almost peaceful. That sounds like the opposite of what Daniel just described.
questions.intent: Position Oliver as the aesthetic counterweight to the political and moral readings — draw out the 'minor key, elegiac acceptance' take and let him make the case that the prose performance is the meaning, not a vehicle for it

questions.question: Okay, Oliver — the 'roar on the other side of silence.' Edmund quoted it too. I want you to read us the closing meditation on Dorothea, because you've been saying this whole conversation that it has to be heard. Let's hear it. And then I want Edmund and Daniel to tell us what they hear differently.
questions.intent: Create a passage-reading moment that resets the conversation — let the prose speak before the analysis resumes; designed to produce genuine emotional texture on air and give all three experts something specific to react to

questions.question: Last one, and I want everyone to weigh in: Daniel, you said Eliot asks us to admire people for accepting their own diminishment and calls it nobility. Edmund says that's not diminishment, that's the human condition. Oliver says it's not either of those things, it's music. So who's right — and what do we do with that final line about the growing good of the world? Does Eliot earn it, or is she letting herself — and us — off the hook?
questions.intent: Force a three-way reckoning on the novel's final moral claim — whether the closing is consolation, capitulation, or something stranger — designed to produce overlapping, unresolved conversation rather than tidy conclusions

steering_notes: This segment should feel like it's building toward something unresolvable — that's the point. Let the Edmund vs. Daniel disagreement run hot early (individual failure vs. structural constraint), but make sure Oliver gets space to reframe the whole debate as a question about what the prose is actually doing emotionally. The passage reading in Q4 is the heart of the segment — protect that moment, don't let it get talked over. End on the 'does Eliot earn it' question and let it breathe; resist the urge to summarize or adjudicate. The best outcome is that listeners feel the tension Eliot herself felt.
cross_engagement_targets: Edmund's claim that 'Dorothea failed herself first' directly contradicts Daniel's structural argument — make sure Daniel gets a full response after Edmund makes this case, not just a brief rebuttal

Daniel's phrase 'convincing good people their diminishment is nobility' should be put directly to Edmund, who will argue this is Eliot being honest about human self-deception rather than exposing a system

Oliver's 'elegiac acceptance, almost peaceful' reading sits in uncomfortable tension with Daniel's 'devastating because it proves the system works' — surface this contrast explicitly after the passage reading

Edmund and Oliver are closer than they realize on the question of individual moral imagination, but they reach it by opposite routes (Edmund: moral responsibility; Oliver: aesthetic performance) — a good follow-up question can make them acknowledge this unlikely alliance
